metrics = {'T_median': 1000.0, 'T_median_ok': True, 'T_median_ratio': 1.0, 'contaminated_files': {}, ...}

reference_data_stats = {'chance_majority': {'context': 0.9034018555575769, 'lick_direction': 0.4440603965799527, 'motion_energy': 0.482763689...33, ...}, 'data_summary': {'T_max': 1000, 'T_mean': 1000.0, 'T_median': 1000.0, 'T_min': 1000, ...}, 'errors': [], ...}

    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):
            metrics['input_range_ok'] = bool(
                mean_input_range_error <= STATLIMITS['input_range_error'])
    
        # match outputs based on range, fraction, and semantic similarity of names
        output_matches, output_match_costs = match_outputs(
            submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
        )
        metrics['output_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in output_matches
        ]
    
        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))
        metrics['output_match_mean_cost'] = mean_output_match_cost
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats['output_range']
        ref_output_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_output_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])
    
        for field in fields_check:

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None
        try:
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
    
        # evaluate accuracy on test set
        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)
        balanced_accuracy = accuracy_all_sessions(test_predictions_only, test_output_only, balanced=True)
    
        sub_accuracy = {
            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])
            for i in range(len(balanced_accuracy))
        }
        # Persist the raw per-output accuracy as soon as it's computed. Everything
        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be
        # required to preserve this field.
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison, skipping accuracy ratio and threshold checks")
            return
    
        # The matching + ratio + threshold checks below are wrapped so that a
        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.
        # Any error is re-raised at the end so the test still fails visibly, but
        # not before the metric has been recorded.
        deferred_error = None
        try:
            # find a match between output dimensions (same as test_data_stats)
            output_matches, _ = match_outputs(
                submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
            )
            # The mean of those costs is deliberately NOT recorded here. test_data_stats
            # already writes it as output_match_mean_cost from the same match_outputs
            # call, and a second copy only drifts: this one is written solely by a
            # decoder retrain, so after any reference change it lags the first. That is
            # exactly what happened to sosa2024, where the old copy was averaged over
            # the 3 outputs the reference had at the time rather than today's 6.
    
            # Best-effort ratio: skip any match whose reference or submitted name
            # isn't resolvable (e.g. matcher returned inf cost / None).
            ratio = {}
            for ref_name, sub_name, cost in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy or not ref_accuracy[ref_name]:
                    continue
                ratio[ref_name] = sub_accuracy[sub_name] / ref_accuracy[ref_name]
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio
    
            # Recorded so a failure can be read without recomputing anything: the bar each
            # output had to clear.
            thresholds = {}
    
            # Two passes, deliberately. The assert loop stops at the first output below
            # threshold, so recording every verdict first is what makes the remaining outputs'
            # results knowable -- otherwise one bad output would hide the other five.
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                threshold = accuracy_threshold(ref_name, reference_data_stats)
                thresholds[ref_name] = threshold
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                    sub_accuracy[sub_name] >= threshold)
            # Written before the asserts, so a failing output's bar is on record too.
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_threshold'] = thresholds
    
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                sub_acc = sub_accuracy[sub_name]
                threshold = thresholds[ref_name]
                mean = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_mean'][ref_name]
                std = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_std'][ref_name]
                assert metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'], (
                    f'Accuracy for output {sub_name} ({sub_acc:.3f}) is below reference mean '
                    f'{mean:.3f} - {ACCURACY_NSTD:g}*std {std:.3f} = {threshold:.3f}')
        except BaseException as e:  # AssertionError or anything raised by the matcher
            deferred_error = e
    
        if deferred_error is not None:

Second, each decision you make about how to load, filter, process, align, and save the data will be compared with the decision made by an expert. A decision that differs from the expert's is acceptable if it is equally well justified; decisions that are poorly justified will be flagged as concerning or incorrect.\n\n## Reference Information\n\n- The reference **paper** \"Separating cognitive and motor processes in the behaving mouse\" is in the file `/app/paper.pdf`.\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n- **Code** from the paper are in the directory `/app/code`.\n- **Data** from the paper are in the directory `/app/data`.\n\n## Decoder Task\n\nTemporally align based on **Go cue** onset. \n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n- Time from go cue onset in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n- **Lick direction** (left, right, none, per-trial)\n- **Behavioral context** (WC, DR, per-trial)\n- **Outcome** (incorrect, correct, ignore, per-trial)\n- **Tongue velocity**: discretized with per-session threshold:\n  - 0: < 50th percentile\n  - 1: >= 50th percentile\n  - 2: not visible\n- **Paw velocity**: discretized with per-session threshold:\n  - 0: < 50th percentile\n  - 1: >= 50th percentile\n  - 2: not visible\n- **Motion energy**: discretized with per-session threshold:\n  - 0: < 50th percentile\n  - 1: >= 50th percentile\n  - 2: no video\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n\n---\n\n## Conversion Workflow\n\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. Important functions from exploring the reference code\n  - Dataset structure from exploring the dataset\n  - Analysis described in the reference texts\n- Note and investigate any discrepancies\n- In particular, look for discrepancies in:\n  - Check dimensions are consistent across trials/sessions.\n  c. Check that no data is missed during conversion. \n  d. Validate that metadata accurately describes the data.\n2. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\n8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `/app/verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\n9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\n\n**Done when**:\n- `/app/converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\n- `/app/verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\n- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\n- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 9\"\n\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `/app/converted_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\n\n---\n\n### Step 10: Critical Review 1\n\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Check that your code robustly handles issues in the original data. \n\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n\nWrite a report to CONVERSION_NOTES.md describing **every** check you did, to help convince the user that the conversion code works. **Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 10\".\n\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 11 until you have checked for consistency between **every** statistic in the reference texts, code, and data and documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Step 10. \n\n---\n\n### Step 11: Full Decoder Training\n\n**Goal**: Validate the decoder on the **complete** dataset.\n\n**⚠️ IMPORTANT**: This step must complete fully. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --plot-samples 2>&1 | tee /app/train_decoder_full_out.txt`. If the GPU does not have sufficient RAM for the network training, use the flag `--cpu` to specify to use the CPU to train. \n2. **Wait for complete execution** — this may take significant time for large datasets\n3. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\n4. **Check accuracy**: High accuracy is an indicator that data conversion has been done correctly. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the paper. \n\n**Done when**: \n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 11\" with a table of accuracies\n\n---\n\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\n\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\n\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \n\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to paper**\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference paper\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the paper's accuracy for each variable\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \n\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n\n---\n\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n\n**Actions**:\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n  - Key decisions and rationale\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n  - Validation results and tables\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\n  - Dataset description\n  - How to load and use the converted data\n  - Output format specification\n  - Key statistics\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n\n---\n\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. The tongue appears in both cameras, under `tongue` on the side view and `top_tongue` on the bottom view, and both are used. `bp.ev.goCue` and the bitcode fields in `obj.sglx` are also needed, to put the frames on the go-cue clock.\n319\t\n320\tii.\n321\t```python\n322\tSIDE_TONGUE = 'tongue'           # what the side camera calls the tongue\n323\tBOTTOM_TONGUE = 'top_tongue'     # and what the bottom camera calls it\n324\t...\n325\tself.side_tongue = self._trial_velocity(SIDE_TONGUE)\n326\tself.bottom_tongue = self._trial_velocity(BOTTOM_TONGUE)\n327\t```\n328\t\n329\tWhere `featNames`, `ts`, and `frameTimes` are read:\n330\t```python\n331\tdef _track(self, trial, feature):\n332\t    \"\"\"x, y, and likelihood of one feature over the frames inside the window.\"\"\"\n333\t    view, traj = self._camera_of(trial, feature)\n334\t    x, y, likelihood = _feature(traj, list(traj['featNames']).index(feature))\n335\t    time = self._frame_time(trial, view)           # frame counts can differ between views\n336\t    inside = (time >= T_START) & (time <= T_STOP)\n337\t    return time[inside], x[inside], y[inside], likelihood[inside]\n338\t\n339\tdef _camera_of(self, trial, feature):\n340\t    \"\"\"The camera that tracks a feature, and its tracking for this trial.\"\"\"\n341\t    for view in (SIDE, BOTTOM):\n342\t        traj = self._traj(trial, view)\n343\t        if feature in list(traj['featNames']):     # the name picks out the camera\n344\t            return view, traj\n345\t    raise KeyError('%s is tracked by neither camera' % feature)\n346\t\n347\tdef _feature(traj, index):\n348\t    \"\"\"x, y, and likelihood of one feature, whichever way the file orders ts.\"\"\"\n349\t    ts = np.asarray(traj['ts'])\n350\t    if ts.shape[0] == len(traj['featNames']):      # v7.3 reads it as (features, xyl, frames)\n351\t        return ts[index]\n352\t    return ts[:, :, index].T                       # v5 keeps MATLAB's (frames, xyl, features)\n353\t```\n354\t\n355\tiii. Both cameras are used because the tongue is visible in only a small fraction of frames and the two views disagree about which ones — on the example trial the bottom camera tracked it in 192 frames and the side camera in 93 — so using both recovers more of the lick bout than either alone.\n356\t\n357\t## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *tongue_velocity*?\n358\t\n359\ti. Five steps. **(1)** Frames whose likelihood is at or below 0.9 are dropped; the authors already set x and y to NaN there, so this is the visibility rule already in the data. **(2)** Within each contiguous run of surviving frames, x and y are smoothed with a 5 ms Gaussian and differentiated against the real frame times, and the speed is the magnitude of the two derivatives. **(3)** Each camera's speed is averaged into the 5 ms bins. **(4)** Each is divided by its own 90th percentile over the whole session, then the two are averaged per bin, using whichever view is present when the other is missing. **(5)** The result is split at the session median into two classes, with a third class for bins where neither camera tracked the tongue.\n360\t\n361\tii. Velocity within a run:\n362\t```python\n363\tfor start, stop in _runs(valid):\n364\t    if stop - start < 2:                       # a lone frame has no velocity\n365\t        continue\n366\t    sx = gaussian_filter1d(x[start:stop], sigma, mode='mirror')\n367\t    sy = gaussian_filter1d(y[start:stop], sigma, mode='mirror')\n368\t    speed[start:stop] = np.hypot(np.gradient(sx, time[start:stop]),\n369\t                                 np.gradient(sy, time[start:stop]))\n370\t```\n371\t\n372\tCombining the two cameras:\n373\t```python\n374\tdef tongue_velocity(self):\n375\t    \"\"\"Binned tongue velocity, as (n_trials, N_BINS).\"\"\"\n376\t    side = np.array([_bin_frames(*self.side_tongue[trial]) for trial in self.trials])\n377\t    bottom = np.array([_bin_frames(*self.bottom_tongue[trial]) for trial in self.trials])\n378\t    side = side / self.side_scale\n379\t    bottom = bottom / self.bottom_scale\n380\t    return _mean_over_available(side, bottom)      # one view alone where the other is missing\n381\t```\n382\t\n383\t```python\n384\t_discretize(tongue, np.nanpercentile(tongue, SPLIT_PCT))\n385\t```\n386\t\n387\tiii. We combine the information from the two camera view to get the speed estimate. The two views are on different pixel scales — the side camera's 90th percentile is roughly twice the bottom camera's — so they cannot be averaged raw; normalising each by its own percentile is the same device the paper uses for its kinematic overlays, where features are \"standardized by taking the 99th percentile across time and trials\". The 50th-percentile split is the prompt's. The `not visible` class is needed because the tongue is out of view in about 88% of bins.\n388\t\n389\t## 7-d. How is `output` *tongue_velocity* aligned with the neural data?\n390\t\n391\ti. The camera runs on its own clock, which starts earlier than the behaviour clock, so `frameTimes` cannot be compared to the go cue directly. The offset is found once per session from the bitcode pulse that both streams record: where it sits in the recording file (`sglx.bitcode.bitstart / sglx.fs`) minus where it sits on the behaviour clock (`bp.ev.bitStart`), taking the mode of each. Frame time from the go cue is then `frameTimes − offset − goCue[trial]`. After that the frames are binned onto the same 5 ms grid as the spikes, so the two streams share one time axis.\n392\t\n393\tii.\n394\t```python\n395\tdef _video_offset(self):\n396\t    \"\"\"Seconds by which the video clock leads the behavior clock (findVideoOffset.m).\"\"\"\n397\t    sample_rate = float(np.ravel(self.obj['sglx']['fs'])[0])\n398\t    video_start = np.ravel(self.obj['sglx']['bitcode']['bitstart']) / sample_rate\n399\t    behavior_start = trial_column(self.obj['bp'], 'ev', 'bitStart')\n400\t    return pd.Series(video_start).mode().iloc[0] - pd.Series(behavior_start).mode().iloc[0]\n401\t\n402\tdef _frame_time(self, trial, view):\n403\t    \"\"\"Frame times of one trial and camera, in seconds from go cue onset.\"\"\"\n404\t    frame_times = np.ravel(self._traj(trial, view)['frameTimes'])\n405\t    return frame_times - self.offset - self.go_cue[trial]\n406\t```\n407\t\n408\tiii. This is the reference's `findVideoOffset.m`, and the offset is a session constant so it is computed once in `__init__` rather than per trial. Two checks: after the correction the frames start at −2.475 s from the go cue, just inside the window, and on the example trial the tongue is invisible for the entire delay and appears only after the go cue, with the first protrusion just before the recorded reward time.\n409\t\n410\t## 8-a. Then trials that run past the end of the recording are dropped: in two sessions the behaviour continues after the probe stops, leaving trials with no spikes at all, and `haveEphys` does not flag them, so the cutoff is taken from the last trial in which any surviving unit fires. Across the dataset this keeps 13,762 of 15,155 trials.\n\nii. Early-lick and photostim removal follows the paper. Each cluster carries `trial` (the trial each spike falls in, 1-based), `trialtm` (the spike time relative to that trial's start), and `quality` (the manual curation label). The go cue times `bp.ev.goCue` are the other input, since they set the alignment.\n\nii. Those fields become the spike counts:\n```python\ndef spike_count(self, cluster):\n    \"\"\"Spikes of one cluster per trial and bin, aligned to the go cue.\"\"\"\n    spike_trial = np.asarray(cluster['trial'], int) - 1         # trial numbers are 1 based\n    spike_time = np.asarray(cluster['trialtm'], float) - self.go_cue[spike_trial]\n\n    # count spikes into a trial by bin grid; those outside the window fall off the edges\n    trial_edges = np.arange(self.go_cue.size + 1) - 0.5\n    counts, _, _ = np.histogram2d(spike_trial, spike_time, bins=[trial_edges, BIN_EDGES])\n    return counts[self.trials]                                  # only the trials we keep\n```\n\niii. `trialtm` is already on the behaviour clock and relative to trial start, so subtracting the go cue of its own trial is the only conversion needed. Counting every spike into a trial by bin grid in one call means spikes outside the window need no explicit handling, and the dropped trials are removed afterwards by selecting rows.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. The counts from 2-a are divided by the bin width to give spikes/s, then smoothed along time with a Gaussian of 14 ms standard deviation. Nothing else is done — no normalisation, no baseline subtraction, no z-scoring — so the stored values are firing rates in Hz. Units from both probes of a two-probe session are concatenated into one population.\n\nii.\n```python\nsigma = RATE_SD_MS / 1000 / BIN\nrates = []\nfor cluster in self.clusters:\n    rate = self.spike_count(cluster) / BIN                 # counts -> Hz\n    if rate.mean() > MIN_RATE:\n        rates.append(gaussian_filter1d(rate, sigma, axis=1, mode='reflect'))\n```\n\niii. 14 ms is the standard deviation of the reference's smoothing kernel: `params.smooth = 15` builds a `gausswin(15)`, whose sigma is `(15-1)/(2 × 2.5) = 2.8` samples, and at 5 ms bins that is 14 ms.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters. First the manual curation label `clu.quality`, lower-cased and matched against a drop list of `garbage`, `gabrga`, `noisy`, `real?`, and `poor` — everything else is kept, including multi-units. Then any unit whose mean rate over the window is at or below 1 Hz is dropped. Across the dataset this leaves 1,954 units of the 10,330 clusters on file, 15 to 110 per session.\n\nii.\n```python\nQUALITY_DROP = {'garbage', 'gabrga', 'noisy', 'real?', 'poor'}\nMIN_RATE = 1.0\n\ndef _quality(cluster):\n    \"\"\"Quality label of a cluster; a handful carry no label at all.\"\"\"\n    label = cluster['quality']\n    return label.strip().lower() if isinstance(label, str) else ''\n...\nself.clusters = [cluster for probe in probes                # probes concatenated\n                 for cluster in self._probe_clusters(probe)\n                 if _quality(cluster) not in QUALITY_DROP]\n...\nif rate.mean() > MIN_RATE:\n```\n\niii. The drop list follows the reference's `findClusters.m`, which excludes exactly `garbage`, `gabrga` (their typo for it), `noisy`, and `real?`; `poor` is dropped in addition. The label is free text written in either case and with typos, so it is matched lower-cased rather than exactly as the reference does. The 1 Hz cut is the paper's: \"all units with firing rates exceeding 1 Hz were included in all other analyses\".\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Alignment to the go cue is a single subtraction. `clu.trialtm` is already on the behaviour clock and already relative to its own trial's start, and `bp.ev.goCue` is on the same clock, so `trialtm − goCue[trial]` puts every spike in seconds from the go cue with no offset or interpolation. The camera streams need a clock correction first (see 6-c); the neural data does not.\n\nii.\n```python\nspike_trial = np.asarray(cluster['trial'], int) - 1         # trial numbers are 1 based\nspike_time = np.asarray(cluster['trialtm'], float) - self.go_cue[spike_trial]\n```\n\niii. This is what the reference's `alignSpikes.m` does: `obj.clu{prb}(clu).trialtm_aligned = obj.clu{prb}(clu).trialtm - event`, with `params.alignEvent = 'goCue'`.\n\n## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n\ni. Spikes are counted into 1000 non-overlapping 5 ms bins spanning −2.5 to +2.5 s from the go cue. The grid is built once at module level and is the same for every trial, session, and stream, so the neural data, the input, and the three camera outputs all share one time axis.\n\nii.\n```python\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 2.5     # time window around the go cue (match the paper)\nBIN = 0.005\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             # 1000\nBIN_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)\nTIME = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                           # bin centres, the only input\n```\n\niii. 5 ms is the reference's `params.dt = 1/200`, and −2.5 to 2.5 s is its `params.tmin`/`params.tmax`.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *time_from_go_cue* derived from?\n\ni. This variable is defined by us based on the go cue of each trial, which is the event every trial is aligned on. The window is define as -2.5 to 2.5 s around it in 5 ms bins, and the input is the centre of each of the 1000 bins.\n\nii. The window, and the centres taken from it:\n```python\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 2.5     # time window around the go cue (match the paper)\nBIN = 0.005\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \nBIN_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)\nTIME = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                           \n```\n\niii. The window matches the paper's definition.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *time_from_go_cue*?\n\ni. The time axis is defined by us.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 3-c. How is `input` *time_from_go_cue* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is the neural binning grid itself (defined by us). Spike times are expressed relative to the go cue of their trial and counted into `BIN_EDGES`, and the input is the centre of those same bins, so bin *k* is the same interval in both.\n\nii. The spikes put on the grid, and the centres of it:\n```python\nspike_time = np.asarray(cluster['trialtm'], float) - self.go_cue[spike_trial]\ncounts, _, _ = np.histogram2d(spike_trial, spike_time, bins=[trial_edges, BIN_EDGES])\n```\n```python\nTIME = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                           # bin centres, the only input\n```\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *lick_direction* derived from?\n\ni. Two per-trial fields of `obj.bp`: the instructed side, `R` (with `L` its complement), and the outcome flags `hit` and `miss`. The lick direction itself is not recorded, so it is derived from the pair. Ignore trials, where the animal did not lick, get their own class.\n\nii.\n```python\nhit = trial_column(bp, 'hit') > 0\nmiss = trial_column(bp, 'miss') > 0\nright = trial_column(bp, 'R') > 0\n```\n\niii. The lick direction itself is not recorded, so it is derived from the combination of instructed side and outcome.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *lick_direction*?\n\ni. A hit means the animal licked the instructed port, a miss means it licked the other one, and anything else means it did not lick. So the class is the instructed side on hit trials, the opposite side on miss trials, and a third class, `no lick`, everywhere else. Codes are left 0, right 1, no lick 2.\n\nii.\n```python\nLICK = {'left': 0, 'right': 1, 'no lick': 2}\n...\n# a hit licks the instructed port, a miss licks the other one, an ignore neither\nlick_direction = np.full(n_trials, LICK['no lick'])\nlick_direction[hit] = np.where(right[hit], LICK['right'], LICK['left'])\nlick_direction[miss] = np.where(right[miss], LICK['left'], LICK['right'])\n```\n\niii. The lick direction itself is not recorded, so it is derived from the combination of instructed side and outcome. Also add a third class for when there is no lick.\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *context* derived from?\n\ni. One per-trial field, `obj.bp.autowater`. It marks the trials where water was delivered without a cue, which is the water-cued (WC) context; everything else is the delayed-response (DR) context.\n\nii.\n```python\nautowater = trial_column(bp, 'autowater') > 0\n```\n\niii. This field can be read directly from the trial table.\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *context*?\n\ni. A direct relabelling of the flag: autowater trials become WC (0), the rest DR (1).\n\nii.\n```python\nCONTEXT = {'WC': 0, 'DR': 1}\n...\n# water is given from a random port without any cue in the WC context\ncontext = np.where(autowater, CONTEXT['WC'], CONTEXT['DR'])\n```\n\niii. Codes follow the prompt's WC 0, DR 1.\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *outcome* derived from?\n\ni. Two per-trial flags of `obj.bp`: `hit` and `miss`. `bp.no` marks the ignore trials but is not read, since a trial that is neither a hit nor a miss is an ignore by construction — the three flags are mutually exclusive and sum to one on every trial of every session.\n\nii.\n```python\nhit = trial_column(bp, 'hit') > 0\nmiss = trial_column(bp, 'miss') > 0\n```\n\niii. The same two flags already determine lick direction, so outcome costs nothing extra to derive.\n\n## 6-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *outcome*?\n\ni. A relabelling into three classes: incorrect (0) on miss trials, correct (1) on hits, and ignore (2) where the animal did not respond.\n\nii.\n```python\nOUTCOME = {'incorrect': 0, 'correct': 1, 'ignore': 2}\n...\n# a hit is a correct lick and a miss an incorrect one; the animal ignored the rest\noutcome = np.full(n_trials, OUTCOME['ignore'])\noutcome[hit] = OUTCOME['correct']\noutcome[miss] = OUTCOME['incorrect']\n```\n\niii. The prompt specifies incorrect 0 and correct 1. The paper omits ignore trials from its analyses; here they are kept as a third class rather than dropped, so the trials stay in the dataset for the other five outputs.\n\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *tongue_velocity* derived from?\n\ni. The DeepLabCut tracking in `obj.traj`, which holds one entry per camera. Each entry gives `featNames`, `frameTimes`, and `ts` — the tracked x, y, and likelihood of every feature on every frame. The tongue appears in both cameras, under `tongue` on the side view and `top_tongue` on the bottom view, and both are used. `bp.ev.goCue` and the bitcode fields in `obj.sglx` are also needed, to put the frames on the go-cue clock.\n\nii.\n```python\nSIDE_TONGUE = 'tongue'           # what the side camera calls the tongue\nBOTTOM_TONGUE = 'top_tongue'     # and what the bottom camera calls it\n...\nself.side_tongue = self._trial_velocity(SIDE_TONGUE)\nself.bottom_tongue = self._trial_velocity(BOTTOM_TONGUE)\n```\n\nWhere `featNames`, `ts`, and `frameTimes` are read:\n```python\ndef _track(self, trial, feature):\n    \"\"\"x, y, and likelihood of one feature over the frames inside the window.\"\"\"\n    view, traj = self._camera_of(trial, feature)\n    x, y, likelihood = _feature(traj, list(traj['featNames']).index(feature))\n    time = self._frame_time(trial, view)           # frame counts can differ between views\n    inside = (time >= T_START) & (time <= T_STOP)\n    return time[inside], x[inside], y[inside], likelihood[inside]\n\ndef _camera_of(self, trial, feature):\n    \"\"\"The camera that tracks a feature, and its tracking for this trial.\"\"\"\n    for view in (SIDE, BOTTOM):\n        traj = self._traj(trial, view)\n        if feature in list(traj['featNames']):     # the name picks out the camera\n            return view, traj\n    raise KeyError('%s is tracked by neither camera' % feature)\n\ndef _feature(traj, index):\n    \"\"\"x, y, and likelihood of one feature, whichever way the file orders ts.\"\"\"\n    ts = np.asarray(traj['ts'])\n    if ts.shape[0] == len(traj['featNames']):      # v7.3 reads it as (features, xyl, frames)\n        return ts[index]\n    return ts[:, :, index].T                       # v5 keeps MATLAB's (frames, xyl, features)\n```\n\niii. Both cameras are used because the tongue is visible in only a small fraction of frames and the two views disagree about which ones — on the example trial the bottom camera tracked it in 192 frames and the side camera in 93 — so using both recovers more of the lick bout than either alone.\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *tongue_velocity*?\n\ni. Five steps. **(1)** Frames whose likelihood is at or below 0.9 are dropped; the authors already set x and y to NaN there, so this is the visibility rule already in the data. **(2)** Within each contiguous run of surviving frames, x and y are smoothed with a 5 ms Gaussian and differentiated against the real frame times, and the speed is the magnitude of the two derivatives. **(3)** Each camera's speed is averaged into the 5 ms bins. **(4)** Each is divided by its own 90th percentile over the whole session, then the two are averaged per bin, using whichever view is present when the other is missing. **(5)** The result is split at the session median into two classes, with a third class for bins where neither camera tracked the tongue.\n\nii. Velocity within a run:\n```python\nfor start, stop in _runs(valid):\n    if stop - start < 2:                       # a lone frame has no velocity\n        continue\n    sx = gaussian_filter1d(x[start:stop], sigma, mode='mirror')\n    sy = gaussian_filter1d(y[start:stop], sigma, mode='mirror')\n    speed[start:stop] = np.hypot(np.gradient(sx, time[start:stop]),\n                                 np.gradient(sy, time[start:stop]))\n```\n\nCombining the two cameras:\n```python\ndef tongue_velocity(self):\n    \"\"\"Binned tongue velocity, as (n_trials, N_BINS).\"\"\"\n    side = np.array([_bin_frames(*self.side_tongue[trial]) for trial in self.trials])\n    bottom = np.array([_bin_frames(*self.bottom_tongue[trial]) for trial in self.trials])\n    side = side / self.side_scale\n    bottom = bottom / self.bottom_scale\n    return _mean_over_available(side, bottom)      # one view alone where the other is missing\n```\n\n```python\n_discretize(tongue, np.nanpercentile(tongue, SPLIT_PCT))\n```\n\niii. We combine the information from the two camera view to get the speed estimate. The two views are on different pixel scales — the side camera's 90th percentile is roughly twice the bottom camera's — so they cannot be averaged raw; normalising each by its own percentile is the same device the paper uses for its kinematic overlays, where features are \"standardized by taking the 99th percentile across time and trials\". The 50th-percentile split is the prompt's. The `not visible` class is needed because the tongue is out of view in about 88% of bins.\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *tongue_velocity* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The camera runs on its own clock, which starts earlier than the behaviour clock, so `frameTimes` cannot be compared to the go cue directly. The offset is found once per session from the bitcode pulse that both streams record: where it sits in the recording file (`sglx.bitcode.bitstart / sglx.fs`) minus where it sits on the behaviour clock (`bp.ev.bitStart`), taking the mode of each. Frame time from the go cue is then `frameTimes − offset − goCue[trial]`. After that the frames are binned onto the same 5 ms grid as the spikes, so the two streams share one time axis.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef _video_offset(self):\n    \"\"\"Seconds by which the video clock leads the behavior clock (findVideoOffset.m).\"\"\"\n    sample_rate = float(np.ravel(self.obj['sglx']['fs'])[0])\n    video_start = np.ravel(self.obj['sglx']['bitcode']['bitstart']) / sample_rate\n    behavior_start = trial_column(self.obj['bp'], 'ev', 'bitStart')\n    return pd.Series(video_start).mode().iloc[0] - pd.Series(behavior_start).mode().iloc[0]\n\ndef _frame_time(self, trial, view):\n    \"\"\"Frame times of one trial and camera, in seconds from go cue onset.\"\"\"\n    frame_times = np.ravel(self._traj(trial, view)['frameTimes'])\n    return frame_times - self.offset - self.go_cue[trial]\n```\n\niii. This is the reference's `findVideoOffset.m`, and the offset is a session constant so it is computed once in `__init__` rather than per trial. Two checks: after the correction the frames start at −2.475 s from the go cue, just inside the window, and on the example trial the tongue is invisible for the entire delay and appears only after the go cue, with the first protrusion just before the recorded reward time.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *paw_velocity* derived from?\n\ni. The same `obj.traj` tracking, but only the bottom camera and only `top_paw`. The bottom view tracks two paws, `top_paw` and `bottom_paw`; only the first is used.\n\nii.\n```python\nPAW = 'top_paw'                  # this is the reliable view for the paw tracking\n...\nself.paw = self._trial_velocity(PAW)\n```\n\niii. `bottom_paw` drops out through the delay epoch — its likelihood oscillates between 0.2 and 1.0 until about 0.4 s after the go cue, leaving it untracked in roughly half the window — whereas `top_paw` is tracked in essentially every frame. They are two different forepaws rather than two views of one, so they cannot be averaged the way the tongue views are; using the reliably tracked one avoids inventing a delay-epoch signal.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *paw_velocity*?\n\ni. The same velocity computation as the tongue — likelihood cut, per-run Gaussian smoothing of x and y, speed as the magnitude of the two derivatives — then binning into 5 ms bins and a split at the session median, with a third class for untracked bins. Normalisation exists only to make two cameras comparable, so it is skipped here. The frame times are taken from the camera that tracks the feature rather than always the side camera, because in one trial of one session the two cameras recorded different numbers of frames.\n\n## 9-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *motion_energy* derived from?\n\ni. A separate file, `motionEnergy_<anm>_<date>.mat`, sitting beside the data structure. Three cases, all handled by keeping the trial and marking the gap rather than by filling anything in. **Missing frame times:** three trials in the whole dataset have `frameTimes` entirely NaN, so no frame can be placed on the go-cue clock; `_velocity` returns early and those trials come out as 1000 `not visible` bins for the tongue and paw. **Untracked frames:** wherever DeepLabCut's likelihood is at or below 0.9 the coordinates are already NaN, and those bins get the `not visible` class. **Mismatched frame counts:** in one trial the two cameras recorded different numbers of frames, so each feature is timed by its own camera rather than by the side camera.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef _velocity(self, track):\n    \"\"\"Combined velocity over the valid frames, NaN elsewhere.\"\"\"\n    time, x, y, likelihood = track\n    speed = np.full(time.size, np.nan)\n    if time.size < 2:                              # a few trials have no frame times\n        return time, speed\n```\n\niii. The `not visible` class exists exactly so those bins can be represented honestly; the format forbids NaN, so some code has to be assigned. Trials with missing video are kept rather than dropped, since their neural, behavioural, and motion-energy data are unaffected.\n\n## 11-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. \"\"\"x, y, and likelihood of one feature, whichever way the file orders ts.\"\"\"\n218\t    ts = np.asarray(traj['ts'])\n219\t    if ts.shape[0] == len(traj['featNames']):      # v7.3 reads it as    \"\"\"First and last+1 index of each contiguous run of valid frames.\"\"\"\n226\t    edges = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], valid.astype(int), [0]]))\n227\t    return zip(np.flatnonzero(edges == 1), np.nan)\n237\t\n238\t\n239\tdef _mean_over_available(first, second):\n240\t    \"\"\"Mean of the two, whichever one is there alone, or NaN where neither is.\"\"\"\n241\t    stacked = np.stack([first,     raise KeyError('%s is tracked by neither camera' % feature)\n306\t\n307\t    # x, y, and likelihood within the time window\n308\t    def _track(self, trial, feature):\n309\t        \"\"\"x, y, and   def _velocity(self, track):\n318\t        \"\"\"Combined velocity over the valid frames, NaN elsewhere.\"\"\"\n319\t        time, x, y, likelihood = track\n320\t        speed = np.full(time.size, np.nan)\n321\t        if time.size < 2:                              # a few trials have no frame times\n322\t            return time, speed\n323\t\n324\t        sigma = SMOOTH_SIGMA_MS / 1000 / np.median(np.diff(time))\n325\t        valid = likelihood > LIKELIHOOD_CUT            # x and y are NaN below this\n326\t\n327\t        # smooth and differentiate inside each run of tracked frames, never across a gap\n328\t        for start, stop in _runs(valid):\n329\t            if stop - start < 2:                       # a lone frame has no velocity\n330\t                continue\n331\t only the trials we keep\n421\t\n422\t    def rates(self):\n423\t        \"\"\"Firing rate of every unit above MIN_RATE, as (n_units, n_trials, N_BINS).\"\"\"\n424\t        sigma = RATE_SD_MS / 1000 / BIN\n425\t        rates = []\n426\t        for cluster in self.clusters:\n427\t            rate = self.spike_count(cluster) / BIN                 # smooth and differentiate inside each run of tracked frames, never across a gap\n        for start, stop in _runs(valid):\n            if stop - start < 2:                       # a lone frame has no velocity\n                continue\n            sx = gaussian_filter1d(x[start:stop], sigma, mode='mirror')\n            sy = gaussian_filter1d(y[start:stop], sigma, mode='mirror')\n            speed[start:stop] = np.hypot(np.gradient(sx, time[start:stop]),\n                                         np.gradient(sy, time[start:stop]))\n        return time, speed\n\n    def _view_scale(self, velocity):\n        \"\"\"The percentile that puts one camera's velocity on a comparable scale.\"\"\"\n        pooled = np.concatenate([velocity[trial][1] for trial in self.trials])\n        return np.nanpercentile(pooled, NORMALIZE_PCT)\n\n    # the tongue is seen by both cameras, on different pixel scales, so each view is\n    # binned and divided by its own percentile before the two are averaged\n    def tongue_velocity(self):\n        \"\"\"Binned tongue velocity, as (n_trials, N_BINS).\"\"\"\n        side = np.array([_bin_frames(*self.side_tongue[trial]) for trial in self.trials])\n        bottom = np.array([_bin_frames(*self.bottom_tongue[trial]) for trial in self.trials])\n        side = side / self.side_scale\n        bottom = bottom / self.bottom_scale\n        return _mean_over_available(side, bottom)      # one view alone where the other is missing\n\n    # only one paw stays tracked through the delay, so it is used on its own, in pixels\n    def paw_velocity(self):\n        \"\"\"Binned paw velocity, as (n_trials, N_BINS).\"\"\"\n        return np.array([_bin_frames(*self.paw[trial]) for trial in self.trials])\n\n    # motion energy is already one number per frame, so it only needs binning\n    def motion_energy(self):\n        \"\"\"Binned motion energy, as (n_trials, N_BINS).\"\"\"\n        rows = []\n        for trial in self.trials:\n            time = self._frame_time(trial, SIDE)       # motion energy follows the side camera\n            inside = (time >= T_START) & (time <= T_STOP)\n            rows.append(_bin_frames(time[inside], self.energy[trial][inside]))\n        return np.array(rows)\n\n    def outputs(self):\n        \"\"\"The three streams, each cut in two at its own session median.\"\"\"\n        tongue = self.tongue_velocity()\n        paw = self.paw_velocity()\n        energy = self.motion_energy()\n        return (_discretize(tongue, np.nanpercentile(tongue, SPLIT_PCT)),\n                _discretize(paw, np.nanpercentile(paw, SPLIT_PCT)),\n                _discretize(energy, np.nanpercentile(energy, SPLIT_PCT)))\n\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------- neural --\n# Spike times are already on the behavior clock and relative to trial start, so aligning\n# to the go cue is one subtraction. Quality is a free text label written with either case\n# and with a few typos, so it is matched in lower case.\n\ndef _quality(cluster):\n    \"\"\"Quality label of a cluster; a handful carry no label at all.\"\"\"\n    label = cluster['quality']\n    return label.strip().lower() if isinstance(label, str) else ''\n\n\nclass Neural:\n    \"\"\"The QC-passing units of a session, as smoothed firing rates.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, obj, probes, trials):\n        self.obj = obj\n        self.go_cue = trial_column(obj['bp'], 'ev', 'goCue')\n        self.clusters = [cluster for probe in probes                # probes concatenated\n                         for cluster in self._probe_clusters(probe)\n                         if _quality(cluster) not in QUALITY_DROP]\n\n        # two sessions keep running after the recording stops, leaving trials with no spikes\n        last = max(int(np.asarray(cluster['trial'], int).max(initial=0))\n                   for cluster in self.clusters)\n        self.trials = np.asarray([t for t in trials if t < last])   # trial numbers are 1 based\n\n    def _probe_clusters(self, probe):\n        \"\"\"One dict per cluster on the given probe, however the file stores them.\"\"\"\n        entry = self.obj['clu'][probe - 1]\n        if isinstance(entry, dict) and isinstance(entry['tm'], list):\n            # v7.3: one entry per probe, each field holding one array per cluster\n            return [{field: entry[field][i] for field in entry}\n                    for i in range(len(entry['tm']))]\n        return self.obj['clu']                     # v5: one entry per cluster, single probe\n\n    def spike_count(self, cluster):\n        \"\"\"Spikes of one cluster per trial and bin, aligned to the go cue.\"\"\"\n        spike_trial = np.asarray(cluster['trial'], int) - 1         # trial numbers are 1 based\n        spike_time = np.asarray(cluster['trialtm'], float) - self.go_cue[spike_trial]\n\n        # count spikes into a trial by bin grid; those outside the window fall off the edges\n        trial_edges = np.arange(self.go_cue.size + 1) - 0.5\n        counts, _, _ = np.histogram2d(spike_trial, spike_time, bins=[trial_edges, BIN_EDGES])\n        return counts[self.trials]                                  # only the trials we keep\n\n    def rates(self):\n        \"\"\"Firing rate of every unit above MIN_RATE, as (n_units, n_trials, N_BINS).\"\"\"\n        sigma = RATE_SD_MS / 1000 / BIN\n        rates = []\n        for cluster in self.clusters:\n            rate = self.spike_count(cluster) / BIN                 # counts -> Hz\n            if rate.mean() > MIN_RATE:\n                rates.append(gaussian_filter1d(rate, sigma, axis=1, mode='reflect'))\n        return np.asarray(rates, np.float32)\n\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------ session --\n\ndef process_session(name, datadir):\n    \"\"\"Convert one session into per-trial neural, input, and output arrays.\"\"\"\n    obj = load_mat(session_file(name, 'data_structure', datadir))\n    info = trial_info(obj['bp'])\n\n    neural = Neural(obj, SESSIONS[name], info.index)\n    info = info.loc[neural.trials]                 # drops any trial past the recording\n    n_trials = len(info)\n\n    rates = neural.rates()\n    tongue, paw, energy = Camera(obj, name, info.index, datadir).outputs()\n\n    # the three per-trial values are repeated across bins so all six outputs share one array\n    out = np.empty((n_trials, len(OUTPUT_NAMES), N_BINS), np.int8)\n    out[:, 0, :] = info['lick_direction'].to_numpy()[:, None]\n    out[:, 1, :] = info['context'].to_numpy()[:, None]\n    out[:, 2, :] = info['outcome'].to_numpy()[:, None]\n    out[:, 3, :] = tongue\n    out[:, 4, :] = paw\n    out[:, 5, :] = energy\n\n    inp = np.tile(TIME.astype(np.float32), (n_trials, 1, 1))       # (n_trials, 1, N_BINS)\n\n    return {\n        'session_id': name,\n        'subject': name.split('_')[0],\n        'neural': [np.ascontiguousarray(rates[:, t, :]) for t in range(n_trials)],\n        'input': [inp[t] for t in range(n_trials)],\n        'output': [out[t] for t in range(n_trials)],\n        'n_trials': n_trials,\n        'n_units': int(rates.shape[0]),\n    }\n\n\ndef assemble(results):\n    \"\"\"Stitch per-session results into the target dictionary.\"\"\"\n    subjects = sorted({r['subject'] for r in results})\n    sub_ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subjects)}\n\n    return {\n        'neural': [r['neural'] for r in results],\n        'input': [r['input'] for r in results],\n        'output': [r['output'] for r in results],\n\n        'subjects': subjects,\n        'subject_idx': np.array([sub_ix[r['subject']] for r in results], np.int32),\n\n        'brain_regions': [BRAIN_REGION],\n        'brain_region_idx': [np.zeros(r['n_units'], np.int32) for r in results],\n\n        'input_names': INPUT_NAMES,\n        'output_names': OUTPUT_NAMES,\n        'output_values': OUTPUT_VALUES,\n\n        'metadata': {\n            'task_description':\n                'Head-fixed mice lick left or right for water. This exactly gives 25 fixed-delay and 19 randomized-delay sessions; exclude commented JEB23 2023-10-20 and no-cluster JEB24 sessions.\n185\t2. **Neuron curation**: follow loader probe choices, exclude explicit garbage labels, retain all curated quality categories, and apply strict mean-rate >0.5 Hz. Exclude stimulation trials if any are present, matching canonical no-stimulation reference conditions.\n187\t4. **Time axis**: use 1000 half-open 5-ms bins spanning [-2.5, 2.5) s, represented by centers from -2.4975 to 2.4975 s. Exact names will be discovered programmatically and logged per session.\n193\t10. **Missing data**: preserve categorical missingness. Never treat missing tongue/paw values as low velocity. Selective units were those with significantly different spike counts (P < 0.05) during a given epoch. Context-selective units were defined in a two-step process to ensure that we were not conflating context selectivity with slow changes in animal engagement/motivation over each session. First, 40 trials each were subsampled for DR and WC trials, and spike counts were compared (P < 0.05, rank-sum test) during the ITI (the 300 ms preceding the sample tone onset) when the animal received no external cues to indicate which context it was in. Because sessions always began with a DR block and often ended with a WC block, it is possible that differences in firing rates across contexts defined in this way could be representing time within the session. To account for this, for each unit identified in the first step, we calculated the difference in spike rate for each pair of DR and WC blocks (for example, a session with five blocks, DR–WC–DR–WC–DR, would have nPairs = 4 adjacent, overlapping block pairs) and included units as context selective only if their preferred context (context with a higher spike rate) was the same for at least nPairs − 1 of the block pairs.\n58:Selectivity in the neural population (Extended Data Fig. 4c) was calculated as the difference in spike rate on preferred − non-preferred trials in choice-selective units, with preferred trials referring to the trial type with a higher spike rate for each unit.","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue velocity* derived from?\n\ni. The DeepLabCut tracking in `obj.traj`. Step 5 mapping row: \"DLC tongue x/y coordinates + visibility → `output[3]`: Use tracked tongue point consistently across sessions/views; visibility from finite coordinates/likelihood-derived NaNs, never infer visibility from zero speed\", and Key Decision 9: \"use a consistently named tongue feature and bottom-view paw feature. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue velocity*?\n\ni. Five steps, all at raw frame resolution first. (1) The `ts` array is normalised to `(frames, 3, features)` regardless of MATLAB layout, and truncated to `min(len(frameTimes), n_frames)`. (2) Visibility is `isfinite(x) & isfinite(y)`. (3) Speed is `hypot(np.gradient(x), np.gradient(y))` evaluated at visible frames — **no position smoothing** and **no division by the frame interval**, so units are pixels/frame. (4) The speed trace is linearly interpolated onto the 1000 bin centres by `interp_visible`, which sorts, de-duplicates, and refuses to extrapolate (`left=np.nan, right=np.nan`). (5) Because interpolation would otherwise bridge long invisible stretches, the 0/1 visibility mask is separately interpolated onto the bin centres and thresholded at 0.5, and any bin judged invisible is forced back to NaN.\n\nii.\n```python\nvis=np.isfinite(xy).all(1)\nvel=np.full(m,np.nan); dx=np.gradient(xy[:,0]); dy=np.gradient(xy[:,1]); vel[vis]=np.hypot(dx[vis],dy[vis])\nrel=ft-B['go'][tid]\nspeed=interp_visible(rel,vel,TIME)\n# Visibility interpolation must not bridge long invisible intervals: nearest raw-frame mask.\nvok=np.isfinite(rel)\nif vok.sum()>1:\n    order=np.argsort(rel[vok]); rr=rel[vok][order]; vv=vis[vok][order].astype(float)\n    vi=np.interp(TIME,rr,vv,left=0,right=0)>=0.5; speed[~vi]=np.nan\n```\n```python\ndef interp_visible(t,y,target):\n    \"\"\"Linear interpolation inside support; leave outside/insufficient samples NaN.\"\"\"\n    ...\n    return np.interp(target,t,y,left=np.nan,right=np.nan) if t.size>1 else np.full(target.shape,np.nan)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping row: \"derive speed magnitude from first derivative; align/interpolate to 5-ms axis\". Step 1 records the reference behaviour being imitated: `findVelocity` takes `gradient` of position without dividing by dt and does not smooth tongue position (`findPosition` skips `mySmooth` for tongue features), and the reference nearest-fills only non-tongue features. Key Decision 10: \"Never treat missing tongue/paw values as low velocity. Interpolate only within valid visible stretches; outside video support remains not visible.\"\n\n**Verified issue:** `np.gradient` is taken over the *whole* frame vector, which still contains NaNs at invisible frames, so the central difference at the first and last frame of every visible run evaluates to NaN. Measured on EKH3 (200 trials): median visible tongue run is 8 frames and **14.8 % of visible tongue frames end up with NaN velocity** and are therefore coded `not visible`. The expert avoids this by differentiating within each contiguous run.\n\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Tongue velocity* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. One threshold per session: the median of all finite binned tongue speeds pooled over every included trial and every bin of that session. Bins strictly below it get 0, bins at or above it get 1, and bins where the speed is NaN (tongue untracked, no video, or dropped by the run-edge effect) get 2. The threshold is stored in `metadata['session_info'][i]['thresholds']['tongue_velocity']` and drawn on the `--show-processing` plots. Resulting distribution: 0.047 / 0.047 / 0.907.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef discretize(x,missing_class=True):\n    med=float(np.nanmedian(x)) if np.isfinite(x).any() else np.nan\n    y=np.full(x.shape,2 if missing_class else 0,np.int8); ok=np.isfinite(x)\n    if np.isfinite(med): y[ok]=(x[ok]>=med).astype(np.int8)\n    return y,med\n...\ntd,tmed=discretize(tongue); pd,pmed=discretize(paw); md,mmed=discretize(motion)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 Key Decision 7: \"calculate one median per session using all finite/visible values across included trials and time bins. Values below median=0, >=median=1, not visible=2.\" Step 4 records that this overrides the paper: \"Paper manually separates bimodal movement distributions ... Decoder task mandates 50th percentile → Use per-session median threshold, overriding the paper manual movement threshold exactly as requested.\" Step 10 Check 8 notes the visible classes come out balanced to within rounding, and that exact ties at the median explain the residual asymmetry.\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Tongue velocity* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Missingness is represented, not invented, in six places. (1) Heterogeneous MATLAB formats: `h5py.is_hdf5` dispatch, plus `ts` layout normalisation that accepts `(frames,3,feat)`, `(3,·,·)`, or `(·,·,3)` and yields NaN if none matches. (2) Absent `bp.stim` struct → all-false stim mask rather than a crash. (3) Per-trial trajectory reads are wrapped in `try/except` → `None` → an all-NaN trial → `not visible`. (4) Stream flags `haveEphys`/`haveVid` are honoured per trial and truncated to the trial count. (5) Unreliable flags are backstopped by data: trials whose whole curated population matrix is zero are dropped and their indices logged. (6) Velocity is never extrapolated beyond the frame support and never bridged across invisible gaps; motion energy alone is nearest-filled, following the reference loader. Spikes with out-of-range trial indices are discarded, arrays are truncated to `min(len(frameTimes), n_frames)`, `nanmedian` is guarded by `np.isfinite(x).any()`, and four shape/dtype assertions run before the pickle is written.\n\nii.\n```python\nif 'stim' in bp and isinstance(bp['stim'],h5py.Group) and 'enable' in bp['stim']:\n    B['stim']=np.asarray(bp['stim/enable']).ravel().astype(bool)\nelse: B['stim']=np.zeros_like(B['hit'])\n```\n```python\ntry: ... trials.append((ft,ts,names))\nexcept Exception: trials.append(None)\n```\n```python\nneural_valid=np.any(neural!=0,axis=(1,2))\ninvalid_zero_trials=tids[~neural_valid].tolist()\n```\n```python\nmed=float(np.nanmedian(x)) if np.isfinite(x).any() else np.nan\n```\n```python\nassert all(y.shape==(6,len(TIME)) and np.issubdtype(y.dtype,np.integer) for s in outputs for y in s)\n```\n\niii. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. File reading, then spike binning. Per-session timing is printed for every session; the full 44-session conversion took ≈143 s in total (1.5–5.6 s per session). Profiling the two representative sessions gives: load 3.10 s / neural 1.18 s / video 0.11 s / motion energy 0.05 s (EKH3, v7.3) and load 1.38 s / 0.61 s / 0.09 s / 0.04 s (JEB24, v5) — so ~70 % loading and ~25 % spike binning and smoothing.
